title: How we perceive revelation: notes, motives, miracles; Acts 13; Luke 23; John 4
source_text: XXXI. At, inquies, quomodo revelationem divinam percipimus? Et unde pendet certitudo fidei qua verbum ipsum Dei amplectimur? Certe Deus loqui non solet quin vox et verbum ejus habeat quasdam notas et indicia, quibus ab humana, vel diabolica impostura et fraude distingui possit atque internosci. Praesertim vero revelatio illa cui fides nostra hodie innititur, et quam habemus in sacris Scripturis consignatam, habet illustria admodum argumenta quibus Deo sese vendicat, sicut thesibus superioribus abunde ostensum est. Neque fides, qua illam suscipimus, est persuasio caeca, et quae sui nullam rationem habeat. Sed qui verbo Dei sicuti par est credit, ad assensum illi praebendum inducitur rationibus et motivis quibusdam, quae viro prudenti suadere possunt revera Deum esse qui loquitur, nec confictam et falsam revelationem pro vera obtendi. Ideoque, praeter argumenta quae ex re ipsa peti possunt, saepe Deus, ut fidem verbo suo crearet, et ad credendum homines compelleret, multa adhibuit signa et miracula, quibus fides eorum qui crediderunt, non raro ascribitur. Ita Sergius Paulus vir prudens, quum vidisset caecitatem qua Paulus Apostolus Elymam Magum percusserat, credidit, admirans super doctrina Domini, Actor. 13. Et Centurio qui Christo morienti astabat, videns mirabilia quae in morte Christi contigerunt, glorificavit Deum, dicens, vere hic homo justus erat: Luc. 23. Similiter Joan. 4. Quum Pater quidam agnovisset filium suum moribundum verbo Christi sanatum fuisse, et convaluisse, illa ipsa hora qua dixerat ei Jesus, filius tuus vivit, et credidit ipse, et Domus ejus tota. Unde merito suspecta est eorum ad fidem conversio, qui conversionis suae rationem exposcenti, nihil habent quod dicant, aut trivialia afferunt.
pass_a_gloss: But, you will say, how do we perceive divine revelation? And from where does the certainty of the faith hang by which we embrace God's Word itself? Certainly God is not accustomed to speak without his voice and word having certain notes and indications by which it can be distinguished and discerned from human or diabolical imposture and fraud. Especially that revelation on which our faith today rests, and which we have consigned in the sacred Scriptures, has very illustrious arguments by which it claims itself for God, as has been abundantly shown in the earlier theses. Nor is the faith by which we take it up a blind persuasion, and one which has no account of itself. But whoever believes God's Word as is fitting is led to giving assent to it by certain reasons and motives which can persuade a prudent man that it is truly God who speaks, and that a fabricated and false revelation is not being held out as true. And therefore, besides arguments which can be sought from the thing itself, God has often, in order to create faith for his word, and to compel men to believe, applied many signs and miracles, to which the faith of those who believed is not rarely ascribed. Thus Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, when he had seen the blindness with which Paul the Apostle had struck Elymas the Magician, believed, marveling at the doctrine of the Lord, Acts 13. And the Centurion who stood by Christ dying, seeing the wonders which happened at Christ's death, glorified God, saying, truly this man was just: Luke 23. Likewise John 4. When a certain father had recognized that his dying son had been healed by Christ's word, and had recovered, at that very hour at which Jesus had said to him, your son lives, he himself also believed, and his whole house. Whence their conversion to faith is deservedly suspect who, to one asking the reason of their conversion, have nothing to say, or bring forward trivial things.
pass_b_english: You will ask how we perceive divine revelation, and where the certainty comes from in the faith that embraces God's Word itself. God does not ordinarily speak without notes and marks in his voice and word by which it can be told from human or diabolical fraud. The revelation our faith rests on today — consigned in the sacred Scriptures — has very illustrious arguments claiming it for God, as the earlier theses already showed at length. The faith that receives it is not a blind persuasion with no account of itself. A fitting believer is led to assent by reasons and motives strong enough to persuade a prudent man that God is truly the one speaking, and that a fabricated, false revelation is not being passed off as true.

Besides arguments taken from the matter itself, God has often used signs and miracles to create faith for his word and compel men to believe; the faith of those who believed is not rarely ascribed to those signs. Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, saw the blindness with which Paul the Apostle struck Elymas the Magician, and believed while marveling at the Lord's doctrine (Acts 13). The centurion standing by as Christ died saw the wonders at Christ's death and glorified God, saying truly this man was just (Luke 23). Likewise (John 4): a father recognized that Christ's word had healed his dying son, and that the boy had recovered at the very hour Jesus said your son lives — and he believed, and his whole house with him. Conversion is therefore deservedly suspect when someone asked for its reason has nothing to say, or only trivial things to offer.
